# The Homunculi

# By

# Grayson Jamis

## 

## Homunculi Legends

Even today, the alchemists of ancient times remain famous for their supposed, but unconfirmed, ability to transmute base metals into gold, using the fabled philosopher’s stone. Less well-remembered, yet even more controversial, is their alleged artificial creation of manikins — tiny living humanoids known as homunculi. Some references to homunculi in alchemical texts featured them as symbolic rather than literal. For instance, the fabled Philosopher’s Stone is sometimes considered to be a homunculus, with its creation no less than the representation of the Magnum Opus process, merely described in a different way.

Some alchemists claimed that the culture medium required for the growth of homunculi contained several biological fluids such as sputum or egg-white, and sometimes inorganic fluids like dew, but the two substances most commonly cited as essential were human blood and semen — both of which are widely believed in primitive Flan societies, no doubt influenced by necromancy, to harbour the vital essence of life. Also required was horse manure, whose heat-releasing properties were utilised to incubate the medium. Bearing in mind that all of the above ingredients are readily obtainable, why was the production of homunculi a skill restricted to alchemists? The answer, it seems, is that the recipes always seemed to contain one vital ingredient that was exceptionally complex and difficult to prepare.

For example, in the homunculus recipe contained within the treatise De Natura Rerum, written by the Suel Transmuter and alchemist Theophrastus Paracelsus, ‘the arcanum of human blood’ was included — essential but esoteric, its constituents known only a few in the alchemical fraternity. Here, just in case any reader wishes to attempt it himself, is Paracelsus’s description of how to create a homunculus:

“Let the semen of a man putrefy by itself in a sealed cucurbite \[glass vessel\] with the highest putrefaction of the venter equinus \[horse manure\] for 40 days, or until it begins at last to live, move, and be agitated, which can easily be seen. After this time it will be in some degree formed like a human being, but, nevertheless, transparent and without body. If now, after this, it be every day nourished and fed cautiously and prudently with the arcanum of human blood, and kept for 40 weeks in the perpetual and equal heat of a venter equinus, it becomes, thenceforth, a true and living infant, having all the members of a child that is born from a woman, but much smaller. This we call a homunculus; and it should be afterwards educated with the greatest care and zeal, until it grows up and begins to display intelligence.”  
![][image1]  
The "arcanum of human blood" is not mundane human blood and the creation of the "arcanum" version is nowhere described. It is obviously the principal component for the formation of this "infant", as later practitioners discovered when trying to use the obvious substitute. The result was expected, mundane and wholly disgusting.

Uneducated witches and warlocks believe that the vaguely human-looking root of the mandragora or mandrake plant Mandragora officinarum inspired could be utilised in the production of homunculi. Legend contends that during his body’s last convulsive spasms before death, a hanged man will sometimes ejaculate semen, and it was said that where this fell to the ground, a mandrake would grow. If its anthropomorphic root was then pulled out before dawn on a Friday morning by a black dog, then washed, and nurtured with milk, honey, and sometimes human blood too, the root would subsequently develop into a homunculus, which would guard and protect its owner. While it is interesting that the concept of the homunculus is shared by alchemists and witches, the arbitrary circumstances of this creation method make it arduous to reproduce by any scientific method.

An even more exotic recipe for growing a homunculus was cited in the year CY 350 by no less a figure of learning than Arinad Christianus from the Transmutation school of Gradsul's Magical Academy. According to his claim, an egg should be taken from a black hen, and a tiny hole should be poked through its shell. A bean-sized portion of the albumen then needed to be removed and replaced by human semen, after which the egg’s opening should be sealed with a delicate membrane. Once this was accomplished, the egg must be buried in dung during the first day of the Planting lunar cycle. After 30 days, a homunculus should emerge from the egg and be placed in a jar filled with pond water and moss. The homunculus would die if exposed for a considerable period to natural air. However, as long as its owner provided the homunculus with a regular diet of earthworms and lavender seeds it would protect him and assist him in all of his endeavours.

Notwithstanding the inherent difficulties in obtaining the necessary ingredients and in performing the intricate series of processes required, records detailing the successful culturing of "homunculi" using this method do exist. An extraordinary specimen grown from distilled human blood and able to emit beams of red light from its eyes was reputedly cultured and exhibited at the court of Tavish II using this method by the royal alchemist Piet Borel.

The most outstanding case, however, must surely be the creation of ten living homunculi in a mere five weeks. This was reputedly accomplished in CY 415 by two Suel sorcerers — a nobleman, the Count of Nimlee, and the powerful sorcerer, Abbé Geloni. Like all homunculi, these ten were sealed jars, which were filled with water and a mixture of horse manure and egg whites. The homunculi were treated with some special, but unspecified, solution, which doubled the size of eight of the homunculi, producing a series of one foot tall specimens. No two homunculi looked the same, and to each was fixed an identity. Eight were physical manikins, known respectively as the king, queen, knight, monk, nun, seraph, miner, and architect, and clothes pertinent to their identities were manufactured for them. Each of these eight homunculi was fed with a special rose-pink pellet every 3–4 days, and their water was changed once a week. On one occasion, the ‘king’ homunculus escaped from his jar, and was earnestly trying to remove the seal on the jar housing the ‘queen’ when he was spotted by the Count of Nimlee's servant. Chased by the count and servant, the ‘king’ soon fainted from exposure to the air, and was put back inside his own receptacle.

The remaining two homunculi were non-corporeal, and only appeared when Geloni tapped their jars and chanted certain magical words. A face would then materialise in each of them; moreover, in one the liquid would turn blue, in the other it would turn red. The red ‘spirit’ homunculus bore a horrible expression upon its face, was fed with a thimbleful of animal blood once a week, and its water was changed every 2–3 days, being replaced each time with fresh rainwater; whereas the blue ‘spirit’ homunculus had a beautiful angelic face, but was never fed, and its water was never changed. All ten homunculi would answer questions concerning future events, invariably predicting correctly the outcomes, and they were observed by many people. These included some very notable personages. Surely, however, such bizarre man-made entities could not really have existed — or could they?  
![][image2]  
Many sages wondered whether these particular examples, at least the eight corporeal ones, were nothing more than large anuran amphibians, such as frogs and toads, brought back by travellers from the Amedio Jungle. Certainly, the collecting and exhibiting as curios all manner of dead and living specimens of exotic, unfamiliar creatures not native to the central Flanness was a very widespread activity in CY 300 to 400\. One likely candidate is the Amedio clawed toad, Xenopus laevis, a common species that is very hardy, can live for up to 25 years, is vaguely humanoid in shape, can be up to one ft or so in length if measured from snout-tip to hind claw-tip, and has big protruding eyes. Moreover, it lives almost permanently in water — thus explaining why the ‘king’ fainted soon after escaping from its jar.

An extremely popular laboratory species as well as a pet, thanks to numerous escapes and deliberate releases, Xenopus laevis is nowadays represented by many well-established naturalised populations existing far beyond its native Amedio distribution range, in countries such as the Sea Principalities and Keoland. Is it possible several Xenopus laevis frogs were used in a clever ruse by these two sorcerers to claim mastery of the homunculus? It would not be the first time that a potent elixir of superstitious fear, religious fervour, and zoological ignorance distilled and decanted during that age had transmogrified a real but little-known, odd-looking creature into something ostensibly arcane and anomalous.

However, two decades earlier, the celebrated magus Joi Dee was rumoured to have created homunculi to assist him in his spying activities on behalf of Keoland's regent, Luschan Sellark IV, with claims that these manikins lurked unseen amid shadows and gloom, listening for incriminating information concerning suspected enemies of the Crown that they would then impart to their creator. Of course, such rumors conveniently ignore a basic tenet of homunculus lore, namely that homunculi rarely survive for very long if taken out of the large glass jars or other strong vitreous vessels in which they have been reared. The homunculi of Joi Dee were fashioned not from human semen or horse excrement, but from clay, shaped in the form of small lizard-like creatures and could exist in any environment for as long as they or their masters desired.

## Logical critique of the Homunculi

I discussed my fascination and thoughts on the legends of the homunculus with one of the most sagacious minds in the Flanaess, my uncle Zafar Azane. His thoughts on the matter were enlightening. He contended that the many of the legends surrounding the creation of homunculus are fascinating folklore, yet they are steeped in myth, superstition and misunderstanding. Other legends were the product of outright fraud perpetrated by clever charlatans intent on improving their reputation and the weight of their purses. However, all of these fantasies had a common source – the original text of the Magnum Opus written by Ujor Udias, the greatest transmuter that lived after the fall of the Suel Empire.

Ujor’s description of the homunculus was recreated from the lost works of the great Selrotin, where the Homunculus is a potent medicament derived through spagyrical art, intended to restore vitality and fortify the human spirit. The Homunculus, as a medicament, is derived from the essential nutrients of life—“bread” and “wine”. These elements are transformed into the life force of man, through a process of digestion and purification, this life force becomes the Homunculus, a metaphorical representation of man's essence. This alchemical creation, once ingested, is swiftly converted into blood and spirit, rejuvenating the body and fortifying the soul. It acts as a powerful remedy against mortal diseases by replenishing the vital spirits, akin to oil fueling a flame. Through this medicament, not only are ailments vanquished, but youth is renewed, and the onset of age is delayed.

According to Zafar, Theophrastus Paracelsus had correctly deciphered the Magnum Opus and had begun using Selrotin’s process to treat the nobles of Keoland for ailments and age. However, the practice was akin to necromancy in the eyes of many of Keoland’s population, as the “bread” and “wine” in the recipe are euphemisms for human flesh and blood. This fact was disguised in the original text of the Magnum Opus to all but learned alchemists, but as Paracelsus expanded this practice this fact became a common secret. Although the Homunculus created by Paracelsus didn’t require the death of the “donors”, Luschan III banned the practice in CY 5\. Paracelsus was denounced as a warlock engaged in necromancy and was burned at the stake for his “heresy”. The following year saw the creation of the Office of Forbidden Magic, founded in Gradsul by Luschan III, to ensure the purity of the magical arts in Keoland.

After the death of Theophrastus Paracelsus, the original text of the Magnum Opus was judiciously edited by the Inquisitors of the Office of Forbidden Magic and the description of the Homunculus was removed because of the supernatural and political peril it posed to the kingdom. The legend of the “homunculus” was created to hide the crimes of Theophrastus Paracelsus and his hundreds of co-conspirators who were all among the Keoish nobility. Zafar believes that the activities of Arinad Christianus, who was a respected sage in the School of Transmutation in Gradsul, was an attempt by the Office of Forbidden Magic to further frustrate the rediscovery of Selrotin’s Homunculus.

As for the homunculi of the Count of Nimlee and Abbé Geloni; Zafar believes them to be nothing more than a fantastical fraud, perpetrated by two talented con-men on the young and impressionable “boy king”, Tavish III. Zafar fully endorsed the theory that Xenopus laevis frogs were used in the ruse.

However, to my astonishment, Zafar informed me that Joi Dee's version of the homunculi was wholly real and wholly practical. Why is Joi Dee's version of homunculi so different from the traditional manifestation of these tiny manikins and why is it so much more useful?

## Joi Dee's Homunculi

Joi Dee's version of homunculi represents a radical departure from the traditional alchemical and mythical interpretations of these tiny manikins. Instead of relying on the esoteric and often grotesque ingredients and processes described in ancient texts, Joi Dee's homunculi are crafted using a combination of clay and magical green crystals. Unlike traditional homunculi, which are often described as living entities with limited lifespans and environmental dependencies, Joi Dee's creations are more akin to automatons. They do not require sustenance or specific environmental conditions to survive, making them highly reliable and versatile spies.

The magical green crystals are the cornerstone of Joi Dee's homunculi. These crystals are believed to be imbued with a form of arcane energy that can be harnessed to animate inanimate objects. The "heartstone" gem is embedded within the clay form of the homunculus, the crystals act as a conduit for the master's will and thoughts, effectively turning the homunculus into an extension of the creator's consciousness.

The homunculi are animated through a ritual that involves focusing the master's intent and channeling it through the green crystals. This process effectively links the homunculus to the master's mind, allowing for seamless control and communication. The homunculi can perform complex tasks, gather information, and even engage in rudimentary problem-solving, all while being guided by the master's thoughts.

The use of clay and magical crystals ensures that Joi Dee's homunculi are not only long-lasting but also resilient to damage. They can be repaired or modified with relative ease using simple mending cantrips, further extending their utility and lifespan.

## Zafar's Instructions

The foundation of these homunculi begins with a malleable clay, carefully sculpted into the likeness of small, lizard-like creatures. This choice of form is not arbitrary; the lizard's form is simple and durable, unlike that of a spider or another insect. Also, with its ability to blend into its surroundings, is an ideal model for a creature designed for espionage. The clay is imbued with a subtle enchantment by soaking it in warm water with one drop of its master's blood, making it receptive to the magical energies that will soon animate it. The form can be as complex or simple as desired, but a true artisan will ensure that the final form is both functional and aesthetically pleasing.

Central to the animation of Joi Dee's homunculi are the green gemstones. The ones gifted to me by the Lithomancer Zafar Azane are similar to the stones used to create the animated blades he is famous for. Zafar has informed me that he learned how to create these stones in the archives of the Arcane Order; a lost variation of a "Soul Gem" whose creation was discovered and perfected by the transmuters of the Suel Empire before the Twin Cataclysms. One stone is known as the "heartstone" and is used to animate the homunculi. The other is the "mindstone", which the homunculi's master will use to animate the automaton. Each gemstone is attuned to a specific frequency of arcane energy, a process that requires both skill and patience. The "heartstone" is embedded within the clay form, nestled where a heart might reside, and it is this stone that serves as the conduit for the master's will, via the "mindstone".  
![][image3]  
With proper gemstones the ritual of animation is simple. The master stands before the nascent homunculus, focusing his mind and channeling his thoughts through the "mindstone". The master intones the magical words, "lapis philosophorum". As the master's consciousness flows into the "mindstone", the homunculus is awakened with a spark of life. This connection is not one of domination but of symbiosis; the homunculus becomes an extension of the master's mind, capable of executing complex tasks and relaying information with uncanny precision.  
![][image4]  
Once animated, the homunculi are remarkably resilient. Unlike their traditional counterparts, they do not wither outside of their jars or require sustenance to survive. Their clay bodies, reinforced by the magical properties of the "heartstones", can withstand the rigors of their missions. Should they sustain damage, a simple mending cantrip is sufficient to restore them to their original state, ensuring their longevity and continued service.

Zafar informed me that this implementation of Joi Dee's method of creating homunculi is but one of many possible paths to animation. These homunculi, unlike their mythical phantoms, are not mere curiosities but invaluable tools, capable of performing feats that would be impossible for any ordinary spy.
